newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda trial hears how accused ordered killings.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda trial hears how accused ordered killings.

text.p: Prosecution witnesses told a Rwandan court on Wednesday how a prominent politician accused of genocide ordered and incited killings during the 1994 mass slaughter.

Froduald Karamira, former vice-president of the Hutu extremist MDR-Power party under the ousted Hutu government, is charged with genocide and crimes against humanity and is the most senior genocide suspect to come to trial in Rwanda.
He is charged under Rwanda's genocide law with Category One crimes and therefore will face the death penalty if convicted.
Witness Gerald Ngendahimana, a servant in the house next to Karamira's, described how the accused reacted when his employer refused to man a roadblock at the start of the killings in April 1994.

"Karamira sent Interahamwe militiamen to the house who looted the house, then shot him and then shot his wife. Then they shot me in the eye," he said showing the court gunshot wounds to the side of his face.
Witnesses said Karamira was a leader of the extremist MDR-Power party and incited violence through radio broadcasts.

"Karamira not only killed people during the genocide but even before. I would say that he caused all the attacks purely through his broadcasts on RTLM (extremist Radio Mille Collines) and all his political announcements through MDR-Power," Safili, a former deputy leader of a moderate wing of MDR told the court.
"He kept saying that the Tutsis were Inyenzi (cockroaches) and shouldn't be allowed into government and that we should rid ourselves of them," Safili said.
Karamira, wearing Rwanda's pink prison uniform, sat impassively in the packed and stuffy courtroom, though he earlier told Reuters he doubted the court's ability to dispense justice.
Around 300 outside the courtroom people listened to a broadcast of the proceedings relayed live via state radio.
The trial will continue on Thursday and four more witnesses will be examined before the judges give their verdict.
Karamira is accused of being a leader of the Hutu extremist Interahamwe militia, one of the main forces that carried out the slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Karamira was born a Tutsi but changed to Hutu using a centuries-old custom which allows people to change tribe.
He was allegedly responsible for inciting genocide through broadcasts on state-run Radio Rwanda and Radio Mille Collines.
He was arrested at Ethiopia's Addis Ababa airport last June and extradited to Rwanda.
At least nine people have been sentenced to death for genocide since trials of the first of some 90,000 suspects crammed into Rwanda's jails started in late December.

The United Nations has an international criminal tribunal for the Rwandan genocide with a maximum penalty of life imprisonment. It has 11 suspects in custody at its Tanzania headquarters. REUTER CMJ MB PWS
